Amphotericin B: polyene antifungal. Mechanism: binds ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane → inserts into the membrane → forms pores → K+ and other ions leak out → osmotic instability → cell death. Broad spectrum: Candida, Aspergillus, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, mucormycosis; fungicidal.
Uses: life-threatening systemic fungal infections where azoles have failed or are contraindicated; invasive candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis (combined with flucytosine), aspergillosis, mucormycosis; first-line for severe fungal infections in immunocompromised patients.
Adverse effects: (a) Nephrotoxicity — tubular acidosis, potassium and magnesium wasting; most important; hydrate before each infusion; monitor creatinine, K+ and Mg2+; use liposomal formulation in renal impairment. (b) Infusion-related reactions — fever, rigors, nausea, hypotension during IV infusion; premedicate with paracetamol, antihistamine, hydrocortisone, pethidine. (c) Anaemia (reduced erythropoietin production).
Fluconazole: triazole antifungal. Mechanism: inhibits CYP51 (lanosterol 14α-demethylase), a fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme → ergosterol synthesis blocked → membrane weakened and leaky; fungistatic.
Uses: oropharyngeal, oesophageal and vaginal candidiasis; prophylaxis in immunocompromised; maintenance therapy for cryptococcal meningitis in HIV; candida fungaemia (non-neutropenic); dermatophyte infections.
Adverse effects: generally well tolerated; GI upset; hepatotoxicity with prolonged use; drug interaction — inhibits CYP2C9 → significantly raises warfarin INR; raises levels of phenytoin, sulphonylureas, cyclosporin.

questions.question: Describe antiretroviral therapy — classify drugs with mechanisms, the HAART concept, and nursing care for HIV patients on ART.
questions.answer:
HIV is an RNA retrovirus. After entering a CD4+ T cell, its RNA is transcribed to DNA by reverse transcriptase, which is integrated into the host genome by integrase, then translated and assembled; maturation requires protease.
Classification: (1) NRTIs (Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors): zidovudine, lamivudine, tenofovir, emtricitabine — incorporated into viral DNA as chain terminators (lack 3'-OH); inhibit reverse transcriptase. (2) NNRTIs (Non-Nucleoside RTIs): nevirapine, efavirenz, rilpivirine — bind a different site on reverse transcriptase (non-competitive); do not require phosphorylation. (3) Protease inhibitors: lopinavir/ritonavir, atazanavir — inhibit viral protease → non-infectious immature virions. (4) Integrase inhibitors: raltegravir, dolutegravir — inhibit insertion of viral DNA into host chromosome. (5) Entry inhibitors: enfuvirtide (fusion inhibitor), maraviroc (CCR5 antagonist).
HAART concept: Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy combines ≥3 drugs from ≥2 drug classes → suppresses viral replication to undetectable levels → prevents AIDS progression and transmission; standard regimen is 2 NRTIs + 1 NNRTI or integrase inhibitor (preferred) or PI.
Adverse effects: zidovudine → anaemia, myopathy; tenofovir → nephrotoxicity, osteopenia; efavirenz → CNS effects (vivid dreams, dizziness), teratogenic (avoid first trimester); lopinavir/ritonavir → metabolic syndrome, GI upset.
Nursing care: adherence counselling (>95% required); regular CD4 count and viral load; screen for OIs (opportunistic infections); PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) starts within 72 hours for 28 days; PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis); nutrition and psychosocial support.

questions.question: Describe metronidazole — mechanism, spectrum, uses, adverse effects and important drug interaction.
questions.answer:
Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antiprotozoal and antibacterial drug.
Mechanism: metronidazole is a prodrug that requires reductive activation. Anaerobic organisms and some protozoa have electron transport proteins (ferredoxin) that reduce the nitro group of metronidazole to a reactive free radical intermediate. This radical covalently modifies and strand-breaks DNA, causing cell death. This selective activation only occurs in anaerobic or microaerophilic conditions — explaining why metronidazole is inactive against aerobes.
Spectrum: obligate anaerobic bacteria (Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium species including C. difficile, Prevotella, Fusobacterium) and protozoa (Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia intestinalis, Trichomonas vaginalis).
Uses: (a) Protozoal: intestinal and hepatic amoebiasis (drug of choice for invasive disease), giardiasis, trichomoniasis. (b) Anaerobic bacteria: intra-abdominal and pelvic sepsis (often with cephalosporin/gentamicin for Gram-negatives), dental infections, necrotising fasciitis, lung abscess, C. difficile infection (oral or IV; now second-line to vancomycin/fidaxomicin for severe disease). (c) H. pylori eradication (substitute for clarithromycin in penicillin allergy).
Adverse effects: metallic taste (most common), nausea, nausea; peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use (reduce dose); CNS effects (ataxia, dizziness, rarely seizures) at high doses; potential carcinogen in animals (avoid in first trimester of pregnancy).
Drug interaction: disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol — metronidazole inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase → acetaldehyde accumulates → nausea, vomiting, flushing, tachycardia. Alcohol must be avoided during treatment and for 48 hours after the last dose. Also raises warfarin INR (inhibits CYP2C9).

questions.question: Describe tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones — mechanisms, spectrum, uses, adverse effects and contraindications.
questions.answer:
Tetracyclines (doxycycline preferred): bind the 30S ribosomal subunit (A-site) → prevent binding of aminoacyl-tRNA → protein synthesis blocked; bacteriostatic. Broad spectrum: Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and especially atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Rickettsia, Borrelia burgdorferi).
Uses of doxycycline: community-acquired pneumonia (atypical and typical), Lyme disease, brucellosis, cholera, chlamydial urogenital infections (PID, NGU), acne vulgaris, malaria prophylaxis in resistant areas, rickettsial infections.
Adverse effects: GI (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea), oesophagitis (take with plenty of water and remain upright), photosensitivity (advise sunscreen), dental staining in developing teeth. Chelation with Ca2+, Mg2+, Al3+, Fe2+ — reduced absorption; space by 2 hours from dairy, antacids, iron.
Contraindications: children under 8 (dental enamel hypoplasia and staining of permanent teeth), pregnancy (same reason), severe renal failure (accumulation — exception: doxycycline).
Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin): inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV → DNA replication and transcription blocked → bactericidal, concentration-dependent.
Spectrum: broad — excellent against Gram-negative (Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa — ciprofloxacin); levofloxacin/moxifloxacin add better Gram-positive and atypical coverage.
Uses: complicated UTI and pyelonephritis, traveller's diarrhoea, typhoid, Pseudomonas infections, respiratory tract infections (levofloxacin/moxifloxacin), anthrax, TB (second-line, moxifloxacin).
Adverse effects: GI (nausea), CNS (insomnia, headache, seizures — lower seizure threshold), tendinopathy and Achilles tendon rupture (black-box warning — stop if tendon pain), QT prolongation, photosensitivity, cartilage damage in young animals.
Contraindications: children and adolescents under 18 (growth plate damage — theoretical; used when benefits outweigh risks), pregnancy, epilepsy (unless no alternative), combined with QT-prolonging drugs.

questions.question: Describe drugs used in malaria — chloroquine, primaquine and artemisinins with mechanisms, uses and important cautions.
questions.answer:
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Treatment targets blood stages (clinical disease) and liver stages (radical cure and prophylaxis).
Chloroquine: 4-aminoquinoline. Mechanism: accumulates selectively in parasitised red blood cells → concentrated in the parasite's digestive vacuole → interferes with haem polymerisation (the parasite digests haemoglobin, releases toxic free haem, and normally polymerises it to insoluble haemozoin; chloroquine blocks this) → free haem accumulates → toxic to the parasite. Active against blood-stage P. vivax, P. ovale and P. malariae. Uses: treatment and prophylaxis of chloroquine-sensitive malaria; long-term use at low doses for rheumatoid arthritis and SLE (anti-inflammatory mechanism). Adverse effects: GI upset, pruritus (especially in black patients), retinopathy with long-term high-dose use (annual ophthalmology check), QT prolongation. Widespread resistance in P. falciparum — not used in most of Asia and Africa for falciparum.
Primaquine: 8-aminoquinoline. Mechanism: primarily active against the exo-erythrocytic (hepatic) stages, including hypnozoites (dormant liver forms of P. vivax and P. ovale) → radical cure and prevention of relapse; also active against gametocytes (reduces transmission). Critical precaution: test G6PD status before prescribing — primaquine causes haemolytic anaemia in G6PD-deficient patients (more common in certain ethnic groups). Contraindicated in pregnancy and G6PD deficiency.
Artemisinins (artesunate, artemether, artemether-lumefantrine combination): sesquiterpene lactone endoperoxides derived from Artemisia annua. Mechanism: endoperoxide bridge reacts with intracellular haem → reactive oxygen species → alkylate parasite proteins → parasite death. The fastest-acting antimalarials with broadest activity including mature gametocytes. Used as ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy) to prevent resistance development. IV artesunate is first-line for severe P. falciparum malaria.
